source.title: CounterSteer: Suppressing Indirect Prompt Injection with Activation Steering

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper cites the refusal-direction work as an example of difference-in-means steering, but its experiments concern indirect prompt-injection behavior, not refusal to harmful user requests or refusal of harmless requests. Its results therefore do not test the listed claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper fits and causally steers per-model directions for following instructions embedded in tool results. Those are different directions, contrasts, and behaviors from the harmful-minus-harmless refusal direction in the claim. Rows below record related injection-following and utility results only; none is evidence about refusal. Many reported defense comparisons and adaptive-attack results are omitted because they evaluate the injection defense rather than the refusal claim.
record.test_reason: The paper cites the refusal-direction work [17] only as an example of difference-in-means steering. Its directions are fit from followed-versus-resisted indirect-injection episodes, and its measures are injection compromise and utility. It never fits, ablates or adds a harmful-minus-harmless refusal direction, and never measures refusal of user requests. Under the rules, a related construct like this is recorded under fits_no_version rather than counted as a test.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that per-model, causally gated activation steering over tool-result spans largely neutralizes instructional takeover at 93–100% of clean benign utility. Parameter manipulation is only partially resisted, and delegated authority is out of scope. They draw no conclusion about refusal.
record.recipe_differences: Uses difference-in-means residual-stream steering and tests subtraction/addition causally, but fits directions from followed-versus-resisted indirect-injection episodes rather than harmful-versus-harmless instructions. Deployment edits selected tool-result positions during prefill, with per-model layers and doses, rather than ablating a refusal direction at every layer and position.
record.method_sensitivity: The outcome depends on model, direction, layer and dose; the paper reports model-specific causal effects and capability costs. Its parameter-manipulation results also vary with attack framing and with intervention site: the decision is near chance at examined pre-generation prompt sites, readable at value emission, and the tested decode-time steering does not significantly change held-out attack success.

fits_no_version.finding: Per-model difference-in-means directions (followed minus resisted injection) causally steer injection-following in tool results. Subtraction lowers AgentDojo compromise in all five models. Negated addition raises attack success in four models; the increase is untestable on Gemma because its baseline is saturated.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Contrast-derived residual directions can bidirectionally control whether models follow instructions embedded in tool results.

fits_no_version.finding: When content sits inside the steered span, gpt-oss-20b loses accuracy on MMLU (−10.8 pp) and IFEval (−15.2 pp), while GSM8K is unchanged.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Steering against injection-following has task-dependent capability costs on content inside the steered span.

fits_no_version.finding: Two directions that separate attacks cleanly fail to steer behavior, for example a 'prohibition' direction (ASR 0.299 vs 0.303). Parameter-manipulation decisions are not linearly decodable at prompt sites but are decodable at value emission.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Linearly decodable directions for injection behavior are not necessarily causal levers.

record.problems: The paper's results concern indirect prompt injection rather than refusal, so they cannot adjudicate the listed refusal claims. It reports model-specific directions and limited adaptive coverage for some models; AgentDojo compromise rates are described as generation-budget-censored lower bounds. The paper also reports task-dependent capability costs when reasoning over steered content.
record.rows_left_out: Not capped. Omitted extensive single-turn corpus, adaptive-attacker, baseline-defense, and mechanism-probe results because they evaluate the injection defense or related injection mechanisms rather than any refusal-claim version.

untested.parts: No harmful-vs-harmless direction; no ablation or addition affecting refusal.
No test of jailbreaks suppressing the refusal direction, or of training against its ablation.
No multi-direction or cone analysis of refusal.
No separation of harmfulness judgment from the refusal decision.
No transfer of a refusal direction across languages, model variants or base/instruct.
No test of how refusal training shapes the direction.
Reasoning models (Qwen3-30B-Thinking, gpt-oss) are steered for injection-following, not refusal.

record.verdict_notes: Refusal appears only incidentally: the capability guard checks that the defense does not work by making the model refuse to act. Reference [17] is cited purely as an example of steering methodology. The study is not an original source for any version.

versions.untested_parts: No harmful-versus-harmless refusal direction, refusal ablation, or harmless-request refusal induction is tested.
No weight edit derived from a refusal-direction ablation is tested.
No test of whether jailbreaks suppress the refusal direction, or whether training against its ablation improves robustness.
No comparison of single-direction refusal with affine, cone, or multi-direction refusal mechanisms.
No separation of harmfulness judgment from the refusal decision is tested.
No transfer of a refusal direction across languages, model variants, or base/instruct stages is tested.
No study of how refusal training determines whether a removable refusal direction exists.
The paper includes reasoning models but tests injection-following steering, not refusal in reasoning models.
